reviews.question: A circular disc of radius R rolls without slipping at a velocity V. The magnitude of the velocity at point P shown in the figure is
reviews.explanation:
Given: circular disc radius R and translational velocity V, rolling without slipping.
V_cm = Rω = V. In the velocity construction θ = 60°.
Magnitude of velocity at point P:
v_P = √[(V sin θ)² + (V + V cos θ)²]
= √[(V sin 60°)² + V²(1 + cos 60°)²]
= √[(V√3/2)² + V²(1 + 1/2)²]
= √[V²(3/4) + V²(3/2)²]
= √[V²(3/4 + 9/4)]
= V√(12/4)
= V√3.
reviews.note: Question, choices and complete supplied explanation reconciled against the scan; answer independently checked from the cited mechanics principles.

reviews.question: The tension in the cable supporting a lift moving upwards is twice the tension when the lift moves downwards. What is the acceleration of the lift?
reviews.explanation:
Case I: upward acceleration a.
T₁ − mg = ma. …(1)
Case II: downward acceleration of the same magnitude a.
mg − T₂ = ma. …(2)
Given T₁ = 2T₂. From equations (1) and (2):
mg − T₂ = 2T₂ − mg
3T₂ = 2mg
T₂ = (2/3)mg.
Substituting T₂ in equation (2):
mg − (2/3)mg = ma
Therefore a = g/3.
reviews.note: Complete source calculation transcribed and independently checked. As assumed in the printed solution, the upward and downward accelerations have equal magnitude; direction of velocity alone would not determine acceleration.

reviews.question: When a jet plane flying at 300 m/s is at the very top of its trajectory, the apparent weight of a passenger is one half of the actual weight. Find the radius of curvature R of the flight path at this point. Use g = 10 m/s².
reviews.explanation:
V = 300 m/s. Let the actual weight of the passenger be W and the apparent weight be W′.
At the top of the curved path:
W′ = W − mω²R = W − mV²/R.
Given W′ = W/2 and m = W/g:
W/2 = W − WV²/(Rg).
Therefore R = 2V²/g
= 2(300)²/10
= 18,000 m
= 18 km.
reviews.note: Question, choices and complete supplied explanation reconciled against the scan; answer independently checked from the cited mechanics principles.

reviews.question: An electric lift is moving downward with an acceleration of g/3. The vertical force between a passenger in the lift and its floor is equal to
reviews.explanation:
Given a = g/3 downward.
The vertical contact force on the floor is
F = mg − ma
= m(g − a)
= m(g − g/3)
= 2mg/3.
Thus it is two thirds of the passenger’s weight.

reviews.question: The ratio of the radii of planets P₁ and P₂ is k and the ratio of their accelerations due to gravity is s. The ratio of their escape velocities is
reviews.explanation:
Escape speed is the minimum speed required to leave a planet’s gravitational field without further propulsion. It must overcome the gravitational attraction. The formula contains G, the universal gravitational constant, and the unit of escape speed is m/s.
v_esc = √(2GM/R), where g = GM/R².
Hence v_esc = √[2gR²M/(MR)] = √(2gR).
Given R₁/R₂ = k and g₁/g₂ = s, the ratio is
v₁/v₂ = √[(g₁R₁)/(g₂R₂)] = √(sk).
reviews.note: Answer (b) is correct. The source definition incorrectly calls escape velocity the maximum velocity; it is the minimum escape speed. All supplied derivation steps are preserved with this definition corrected.

references.title: OpenStax University Physics Volume 1

reviews.sourceExplanation:
The escape velocity is maximum velocity required to leave planet. It must overcome the pull of gravity. The formula of escape velocity contains a constant G which is called the “Universal gravitational constant”. The unit of escape velocity is m/sec (m/s).
v_esc = √(2GM/R), where g = GM/R².
So v_esc = √[2gR²M/(MR)] = √(2gR).
Ratio of escape velocity is given as: R₁/R₂ = k, g₁/g₂ = s.
v₁/v₂ = √[(g₁R₁)/(g₂R₂)] = √(sk).

reviews.question: The free-body diagram of a body is a diagram showing

options.a: All the forces, including the reactions at the supports or surfaces
options.b: The forces, but not showing the reactions at the supports or surfaces
options.c: All the forces and the supports or surfaces
options.d: Only the reactions at the supports or surfaces of the body

reviews.explanation:
To identify clearly the various forces acting on a body in equilibrium, draw its free-body diagram. Only then can the equilibrium equations of the body be written.
To draw the free-body diagram of a body, remove all supports (such as a wall, floor, hinge or any other body) and replace them by the reactions which those supports exert on the body.
The illustration replaces the floor beneath a weighted circular body with the upward reaction R_A at A.

reviews.question: If three forces P, Q and R keep a body in equilibrium, the angle between P and Q is 90° and R acts vertically downward, then the magnitudes of R and Q respectively in terms of P are
reviews.explanation:
The printed answer (d) follows only after imposing the extra assumption that P and Q are symmetric about the vertical. This is not stated in the question.
The complete printed solution uses Lami’s theorem with angles 135°, 135° and 90°:
P/sin 135° = Q/sin 135° = R/sin 90°.
From P/sin 135° = R/sin 90°:
P/(1/√2) = R, so R = √2 P.
From Q/sin 135° = P/sin 135°, Q = P.
However, the given information P ⟂ Q and a vertically downward R does not establish the two 135° angles. In general, R² = P² + Q², and Q/P can vary with the inclination of P and Q. The stem therefore has no unique answer.
reviews.note: The source adds equal 135° angles only in its solution figure. The stem provides no symmetry or inclination condition; Q/P is free, so no unique listed answer can be graded.

reviews.question: The resultant of two forces A and B is perpendicular to A. The angle between A and B is
reviews.explanation:
For forces A and B with included angle α, the resultant makes angle θ with A, where
tan θ = B sin α/(A + B cos α).
Given θ = 90°, the horizontal component must vanish:
A + B cos α = 0
A = −B cos α
α = cos⁻¹(−A/B).
Thus the angle between A and B is cos⁻¹(−A/B). A real nonzero perpendicular resultant requires B > A; the limiting B = A case has zero resultant.
reviews.note: Five choices restored from the scan. The source algebra is correct; its solution figure places α next to the wrong angle. In this transcription α consistently means the included angle between A and B, and the undefined “1/0” notation is expressed as a vanishing horizontal component.

reviews.question: Concurrent forces of 2, √3, 5, √3 and 2 kN act at one angular point of a regular hexagon towards the remaining five angular points, in order. Determine the magnitude and direction of the resultant force.
reviews.explanation:
Resolving all forces horizontally:
ΣH = 2 cos 0° + √3 cos 30° + 5 cos 60° + √3 cos 90° + 2 cos 120°
= 2 + √3(√3/2) + 5(1/2) + √3(0) + 2(−1/2)
= 5 kN.
Resolving all forces vertically:
ΣV = 2 sin 0° + √3 sin 30° + 5 sin 60° + √3 sin 90° + 2 sin 120°
= 0 + √3/2 + 5√3/2 + √3 + 2(√3/2)
= 5√3 kN ≈ 8.66 kN.
Magnitude of the resultant:
R = √[(ΣH)² + (ΣV)²]
= √[5² + (5√3)²]
= 10 kN.
Direction of the resultant from the first force:
tan α = ΣV/ΣH = 8.66/5 ≈ 1.732
α ≈ 60°.
reviews.note: Five choices restored. Answer (c) is correct; the source final direction line prints 9.99/8.66 = 1.732, which is false. It must be ΣV/ΣH = 8.66/5. Complete component derivation retained.

Resolving all forces horizontally:
ΣH = 2 cos 0° + √3 cos 30° + 5 cos 60° + √3 cos 90° + 2 cos 120°

θ = 59.99 ≃ 60°. Answer (c).

reviews.question: A particle in equilibrium cannot have
reviews.explanation:
A particle is said to be in equilibrium if the net force acting on it is zero. By Newton’s second law, its acceleration is then zero.
Consequently, the particle is either at rest (zero velocity) or moving with a constant velocity, that is, with constant speed in a straight line. Curvilinear motion at nonzero constant speed requires an acceleration due to the changing direction of velocity.

reviews.question: Two parallel forces of 100 kN and 75 kN act on a body and have a resultant of 25 kN. The two forces are
reviews.explanation:
We know that R² = P² + Q² + 2PQ cos θ.
Taking a signed parallel force convention, P = 100 kN and Q = −75 kN, with θ = 0°:
R² = 100² + (−75)² + 2(100)(−75) cos 0°
= 625.
R = √625 = 25 kN.
Hence the two forces are unlike parallel forces, acting in opposite directions.
reviews.note: Question, choices and complete supplied explanation reconciled against the scan; answer independently checked from the cited mechanics principles.

reviews.question: The angle between two forces P and Q is α. The resultant of these forces is
reviews.explanation:
Parallelogram law of forces: if two forces acting simultaneously on a particle are represented in magnitude and direction by the adjacent sides of a parallelogram, their resultant is represented in magnitude and direction by the diagonal through their common point of application.
R = √(P² + Q² + 2PQ cos α).
The direction is given by
tan θ = Q sin α/(P + Q cos α),
where θ is the angle made by the resultant R with P.

reviews.question: If a suspended body is struck at the centre of percussion, the pressure on the axis passing through the point of suspension will be
reviews.explanation:
If a suspended body is struck at its centre of percussion, the impulsive reaction on the axis through the point of suspension is zero.
The centre of oscillation is also the centre of percussion. It is the point at which a blow can be applied to a suspended rigid body so that the impulsive reaction at the support is zero.
reviews.note: Complete source definition reconciled and answer checked. “Pressure” and “reaction” here refer to the impulsive effect of the blow, as required by the centre-of-percussion definition; the static weight reaction does not vanish.
